facts.raw_span: progressive unilateral skin hardening on his right thigh and buttock for 7 years
motion of his right limb joint was slightly limited
ill-defined, stony-hard plaque involving his right thigh above the patella extending to his right buttocks with loss of skin elasticity
mild hypertrichosis and hyperpigmentation
Normal results for routine blood tests
Normal results for autoantibodies, immunoglobulins, C-reactive protein, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate
Demonstrated slight thickening of subcutaneous tissue and T2 signal abnormality
Normal epidermis and mild pigmentation along the basal layer with subtle increase in density of fibroblasts extending to the subcutis and forming adipocyte entrapment but no evidence of inflammation
Dense reticular dermis extended below well-preserved appendages
Increased expression of CD34 in the reticular dermis
Negative Alcian blue staining

concepts.why: The patient's progressive unilateral skin hardening, ill-defined stony-hard plaque, and loss of skin elasticity are consistent with scleroderma, which is further supported by the histopathological findings of dense reticular dermis and increased expression of CD34 in the reticular dermis.

The patient's skin hardening, hypertrichosis, and hyperpigmentation, along with the histopathological findings of adipocyte entrapment and dense reticular dermis, are consistent with lipodermatosclerosis.
The patient's unilateral skin hardening and plaque, along with the histopathological findings of dense reticular dermis, are consistent with morphea, a form of localized scleroderma.

The patient's skin hardening, hypertrichosis, and hyperpigmentation, along with the imaging findings of subcutaneous tissue thickening, are consistent with panniculitis, although the lack of inflammation on histopathology makes this diagnosis less likely.

The patient's skin hardening and plaque, along with the imaging findings of subcutaneous tissue thickening, are consistent with fasciitis, although the histopathological findings do not strongly support this diagnosis.
It explains the increased expression of CD34 in the reticular dermis, which is a characteristic finding in scleroderma-like disorders.

rationales.F01: Unilateral skin hardening is more typical of morphea than scleroderma.
rationales.F03: The presence of a stony-hard plaque is highly suggestive of morphea.
rationales.F08: The histopathological findings of dense reticular dermis and adipocyte entrapment are characteristic of morphea.
rationales.F09: The extension of dense reticular dermis below well-preserved appendages is a feature of morphea.

frontier_selector.rationale: Morphea best explains the progressive unilateral skin hardening, ill-defined plaque, and loss of skin elasticity, with supportive histopathological findings of normal epidermis, mild pigmentation, and increased density of fibroblasts, without evidence of inflammation.
